claims.title: How accurately must a rectangular Frobenius equation hold?
claims.hypotheses: In the integral crystalline ring, the rectangular error is zero modulo the parameter; its Frobenius recursion has entrywise error divisible by a sufficiently high power of ℓ. Fix the loss c and the desired precision M.
claims.statement: There is an input precision independent of the two ranks for which the initial error is divisible by ℓ^M.

claims.title: Where does the exponent 3H enter the comparison of two sections?
claims.hypotheses: Two height-H frames have integral normalized sections using the same exponent. The rectangular comparison intertwines the two coefficient matrices modulo a sufficiently large power of ℓ.
claims.statement: The moving evaluation composed with the layer section agrees modulo ℓ^M with the target section composed with the constant evaluation.

claims.title: How does a comparison of two frames descend to their integral period matrices?
claims.hypotheses: At a chosen precision, integral crystalline-frame bases have a rectangular comparison in the Witt ring of the tilt field, with one height and one primitive period.
claims.statement: Divisibility descends to the appropriate smaller rings. The projected integral period matrices agree to any prescribed precision with the target matrix times the constant evaluation.

claims.title: How can one integral matrix represent either direction of Frobenius?
claims.hypotheses: Fix a crystalline frame of height H, its common section exponent κ, and the two nonnegative iterates associated to one signed absolute Weil exponent.
claims.statement: An explicit integral matrix V and scalar s satisfy Vφ₂(U)=sφ₁(U). The same s is a unit after localization and works independently of the lattice rank.

claims.title: Why do the integral operators agree after projection?
claims.hypotheses: The target and layer frames have common height, a rectangular link at arbitrarily fine precision, and the iterates fix the unramified base coefficients.
claims.statement: At every precision M one can choose a layer of index at least M whose integral operator commutes with projection modulo ℓ^M.

claims.title: How does a column of a period matrix give a period of the representation we want?
claims.hypotheses: Fix a finite local coefficient model and integral lattice action that reads the matrix columns equivariantly. U is an invertible crystalline period matrix for that lattice.
claims.statement: Each physical column of the matrices paired with a period column gives a Galois-fixed semistable tensor. Its Frobenius iterates and their componentwise evaluation have explicit coordinates.

claims.title: How does the Weil action change the Frobenius exponent in those coordinates?
claims.hypotheses: Potential semistability gives an invertible Frobenius on the period space. Fix a complex coefficient identification and a Weil element of exponent α=n₂−n₁.
claims.statement: The coordinate map factors through the complex quotient imposing the unramified scalar relations. The Weil action takes the class of φ^n₂(m) to the class of φ^n₁(m) for a semistable invariant period m.

claims.title: How can we read a trace from vectors that reconstruct the identity?
claims.hypotheses: A k-vector space of dimension a has additive coordinates in S^a compatible with a ring map from k to the commutative ring S. Fixed finite weights recover each standard coordinate vector.
claims.statement: For any linear operator, summing the transformed coordinates on the diagonal with the same weights gives the image of its trace.

claims.title: Which trace does the integral operator actually measure?
claims.hypotheses: Use a crystalline finite coefficient model of positive dimension a, a rank-d integral matrix lattice that represents the a-by-a identity, its invariant period basis and an operator with Vφ₂(U)=sφ₁(U).
claims.statement: For each unramified-linear functional λ, the ordinary basis traces evaluated against Ve sum to s times the tested local Weil trace. The formula applies to the target and separately to every auxiliary component.
